Tactile- and force-aware manipulation architectures

19 designs, ranked by how far each closes the loop between predicted and measured contact.

Weekly update, 15 September 2026 · compiled 13 September

Architectural evolution

The two lineages started at opposite ends. The vision-language-action family fed touch and force in as extra inputs, while the world-model family predicted touch as an output. They meet in the bottom row, where a model checks live touch against its own forecast.

Most designs fork independently off a backbone in the top row rather than off each other, which is why so few arrows are drawn. Ranks come from four questions asked of every design:

  • C1 Does it predict the contact it expects to sense, rather than command a force it wants?
  • C2 Does it use live touch within an action chunk?
  • C3 Does it read that live touch against its own prediction?
  • C4 Does it scale, in pretraining data and in generality beyond one task?

C1 to C3 set the tier. Tier 1 predicts contact and acts on the gap between that forecast and what it feels; Tier 2 reacts fast to live touch with nothing to check it against; Tier 3 forecasts, then runs the chunk open-loop; Tier 4 reads touch or force and forecasts nothing. C4 orders papers within a tier. A design sits in the furthest row it reaches, so the rows are neither exclusive nor cumulative: every Tier 1 design also reads touch as an input, HiTac-WAM reaches Tier 1 by aborting rather than correcting, and Tier 2 holds one design that forecasts nothing beside one that forecasts richly.

Supporting detail

All the linkages · what each family took, where they cross, and where the forecast comes from

The closed loop did not arrive last. OmniVTA reached it in March 2026, three months before FAWAM and six before TacPAC, coming not from a video backbone at all but from diffusion-policy stock, as TacForeSight did.

The crossover. DeCAL is the one design in which the VLA lineage takes the world-model move outright: a generation expert imagines future visual and tactile latents and the action expert reads them. It reaches that independently, since its stated base is InternVLA-A1-3B and it names no world-model paper in this set.

The loop was already there in Tier 4. Tabero-VTLA and FAWAM make the most useful comparison in this set, because they perform the identical operation on a different input. Tabero-VTLA corrects position from a force error, Δp = kpadm · (Fgriptarget − F̃grip), in which the target is a setpoint the policy emits and the tilde marks an exponentially smoothed measurement. FAWAM computes a residual from a force/torque error, e_w = w_meas − w_pred, in which the target is the world model's forecast. What Tier 1 added was a predicted target and a learned residual in place of a fixed gain. HiTac-WAM puts a calibrated threshold on the same residual, which turns a continuous correction into a replan trigger.

Where the forecast comes from cuts across the rows and sets the order within Tier 3. Some designs denoise touch and action in a single pass (Dream-Tac, Tactile-WAM, VT-WAM, DeCAL), so their action tokens see a target-derived future that deployment will not supply. Others read from a separate predictor (TacForeSight, TouchWorld, UniTacVLA), which cannot leak that way. TacWAM's shortcut result therefore bites the first group alone, which is why TacForeSight outranks designs with larger headline numbers.

Ranking detail · the four questions scored per paper, and what breaks the ties

Each paper uses its own robot, sensor suite and task set, and only UniVTAC is shared, by two of them. Every number below is read from the paper itself rather than from a summary.

The reading set also holds four surveys, two benchmarks (UniVTAC, SoftVTBench) and one sensing-representation paper (N0-Foundation), all held for the next pass.

Ties break on head-to-head results wherever one paper evaluated another on its own setup, with one caveat: a re-run baseline drops sharply. T-Rex 65% becomes 48% in TacPAC, VT-WAM 71.7% becomes 37.5% in TacWAM, ForceVLA 60.5% becomes 35% in ForceVLA2, and the T-Rex pair crosses embodiments entirely. No ordering here is a measured gap. Four papers also award partial credit rather than binary success, and at 16 to 50 trials per cell a ten-point gap is inside noise.

What the forecast is actually worth

Four papers measure the value of a contact forecast, and they disagree only until the forecast is separated from the operation applied to it. Conditioning on one buys almost nothing: ReTouch's forecast, held fixed and used only to condition re-inference, is worth 0.8 points. Refreshing it buys 15.2, and ReTouch carries that claim because it varies nothing else. Training the model to predict contact at all buys 17.5 in FAWAM, 56.25 against 73.75, with no corrector in either row; adding its corrector is worth a further 11.25, though that row also adds 20 human-intervention episodes. TacPAC and OmniVTA agree in direction, 17.0 points from cache access alone and 14 points on wiping, but neither should be leaned on: TacPAC's gap is t(4) = 2.64 with p of about 0.058, Plug supplying 40 of its 85 points, and OmniVTA's figure covers a single task.

Tier 1: predict contact, then correct against the prediction

  • TacPAC (#1) Its comparison is learned inside attention. Its reactive variant is the sharpest evidence in the set: with no expectation to read against, it falls below the vision-only model, 45% against 60% and 25% against 30%.
  • OmniVTA (#2) Its 4-to-1 chunk-aligned correspondence is why it ranks above N0-TWAM, which lets predicted and observed touch meet in one expert without ever pairing them. It ranks below TacPAC because its ablation removes the whole controller rather than isolating the comparison.
  • N0-TWAM (#9) The largest system here, 7.2B parameters over 30k hours, and the only one whose forecast carries physical force units. It ranks top of Tier 3 on scale alone: chunks are denoised while the previous one executes, so the live reading conditions the next chunk rather than the one running, and the paper predicts touch in latent space while observing it in force space, which leaves no comparison to make.
  • ReTouch (#3) Its ablation is the most informative in the set: freezing the forecast costs 15.2 points, deleting it altogether only 16.0. The forecast is worth having almost entirely because it is kept current.
  • HiTac-WAM (#4) It has the most formal comparison, a discrepancy thresholded against a kernel density estimate. It ranks below the three above on C2, since deviation triggers retreat and replan rather than continuous correction, and on breadth, three tasks with per-task tactile modules.
  • UniTacVLA (#5) It has the full structure, but the correction is a small tanh-bounded residual and there is no force/torque sensing. Its own ablation puts the controller at 10 points on top of 16 from the prediction.
  • FAWAM (#6) One of only two designs that write the comparison as an explicit equation, earning 11.25 points for that corrector. A six-axis force/torque reading is a coarse stand-in for the contact field, which is why C1 is only partial.

Tier 2: react fast, without contact foresight in the fast loop

  • T-Rex (#7) By far the strongest priors, 22,889 hours of human video. But it forecasts visual latents only, so the fast expert reacts only once an error appears. No baseline receives its 100-hour mid-training set, worth 20 of the 30-point gap.
  • TouchWorld (#8) The fullest hierarchy, but the predicted subgoal is not an input to its refinement policy, so the 30 Hz loop is blind to the forecast by construction. The world model refreshes only on subtask change, which is why C1 is partial.

The order of these two is the one judgement call that turns on weighting. TouchWorld has some foresight where T-Rex has none; T-Rex has decisive scale where TouchWorld has six tasks. Weighting foresight over scale would swap them.

Tier 3: predict contact, then execute the chunk open-loop

Reading these seven in full changed their order. The distinction that looked decisive from the summaries, whether the action head is allowed to read the forecast, turns out to be near-universal: DeCAL, VT-WAM, Dream-Tac and Tactile-WAM all let action tokens attend to future tactile tokens, TacForeSight consumes a finished forecast from a frozen predictor, and only TacWAM blocks it. What separates them is how the forecast is consumed, and whether anyone checked that consuming it helps.

  • DeCAL (#10) It leads on evidence rather than mechanism: a tactile latent decodable to 6-DoF force, live at inference, and the tier's cleanest margin over a published specialist, 70.8% against DECO at 55.8%. Against that, 600 demonstrations and no tactile pretraining.
  • TacForeSight (#11) The tier's most under-rated entry. The only design fusing wrist force/torque with fingertip touch, and the only one here whose tactile pretraining uses a corpus beyond its own demonstrations. Because its predictor is frozen and run separately, it sidesteps the shortcut TacWAM identifies below. Removing the forecast drops wiping from 100% to 65%.
  • TacWAM (#12) The richest tactile target here, and it then refuses to let action tokens read it, reporting that exposure creates a shortcut when training supplies target-derived futures and deployment generated ones. That holds for its noised-teacher setup but not for designs that regress the future identically at training and test.
  • VT-WAM (#13) Skips future video at inference, which makes it cheap, and its ablation confirms the full tactile sequence is load-bearing. Its latent decodes to deformation rather than force, and half its tasks are scored with partial credit.
  • Dream-Tac (#14) The simplest design that works, and its contact gate needs no privileged information at inference. It beats ForceVLA on five of six tasks, 83.3% against 50.8%, and 100% against 55% when vision is occluded.
  • Tactile-WAM (#15) The cleanest diagnosis of the modality problem: naive tactile injection scores below the vision-only model it extends, and the mask recovers about three quarters of the gain. It ranks low on evidence, losing to π0.5 on both simulation suites, which the paper attributes to π0.5 starting from released weights.
  • VTAM (#16) It introduced the move the lineage rests on, touch as an extra video view, with no force/torque sensor. It drops to the bottom of the tier because the virtual force is an output rather than an input, it never states the action head consumes a predicted tactile state, and inference runs at 1 Hz against 30 Hz execution.

Tier 4: reads force or touch, forecasts nothing

  • ForceVLA2 (#17) The best of this group, and its emitted target forces are this tier's one contribution to the designs above. But it never states what executes the commanded force, and its conclusion misreports its own baseline table. It is the only paper in the set rated weak.
  • Tabero-VTLA (#18) The only design whose sub-chunk predicted-versus-measured force loop is classical, a fixed admittance controller, which is why its comparison is marked as servo tracking rather than a learned check. It sits this low on no real-robot evaluation and no external baseline.
  • ForceVLA (#19) The origin point: force as an input only, and no forecast. It loses head-to-head to FAWAM and ForceVLA2. Its limitations section is the most candid in the group, conceding an estimated rather than a measured force/torque reading.

The contested cell, revisited

The apparent standoff between TacWAM and DeCAL dissolves on a full reading: the two did not run the same experiment. TacWAM's Attn-AT variant grants action tokens the full future tactile sequence and success falls from 55.0% to 37.5%, but those futures are noised teacher targets, target-derived in training and model-generated at test. DeCAL's action expert conditions on directly regressed hidden states, identical at training and at test, so TacWAM's mismatch has no purchase there. Nor is DeCAL evidence against TacWAM, since it never runs a configuration in which the predictions exist but the action expert cannot read them. Tactile-WAM sits on DeCAL's side, making the tally two to one, but all three studies are underpowered at 20 trials per cell, TacWAM's own row being 15 of 40 against 22 of 40, p of about 0.178. The question turns on how the future is produced, and no paper here has tested it at a sample size able to answer. TacForeSight sidesteps it by freezing its predictor.

Ranks are architectural judgements, not a leaderboard: success rates are not comparable across these papers.

Contact-rich benchmarks

Four benchmarks, one toolchain. All build their task environments on Isaac Sim or Isaac Lab, three of them rendering GelSight-style images through TacEx, and N0-Foundation's NeoSim is built on UniVTAC in turn. None of the four releases a simulator of its own.

Two things the grid leaves out. N0-Foundation reports that every policy scores lower on its eight dual-arm tasks than on its four single-arm ones, the best score on Place Gears reaching 18%. The four also differ in what they admit. SoftVTBench states plainly that it does not claim transfer from its simulated touch to real sensors. Tabero concedes that gentleness and reliability are not jointly optimised, and its real-robot collection system is still being built. UniVTAC has no limitations section, though an appendix reports that tactile recovery fails under large offsets.

Supporting detail

Benchmark gaps · what these four do not yet measure
  • Thin sim-to-real validation. SoftVTBench and Tabero never leave simulation. UniVTAC validates on three real tasks. N0-Foundation ranks Fast-WAM among its three strongest real policies, yet it scores 0% on all twelve simulated tasks.
  • One sensor family. All four render camera-based GelSight-style pads on parallel jaws, so the hardware-agnostic claims made for N0-Foundation’s force field and Tabero’s marker field go untested.
  • Incompatible quality metrics. N0-Foundation scores milestone progress, SoftVTBench deformation-capped success, Tabero grip and applied force, UniVTAC nothing beyond success. None measures incipient slip or contact stability over time.
  • Narrow skill coverage. SoftVTBench is pick-and-place only, Tabero evaluates nine pick-and-place tasks, UniVTAC eight insertion and lifting tasks. Sliding, in-hand reorientation and sustained wiping are absent.
  • Uncontrolled tactile necessity. Only SoftVTBench crosses touch with grip granularity, where finer control alone matches touch in distribution. N0-Foundation’s no-touch control gains 6.0 points on one backbone. UniVTAC bundles touch with pretraining, and Tabero’s no-touch row also drops force supervision.
  • Little distribution shift. Only SoftVTBench shifts test conditions, varying lighting, mass and stiffness; Tabero varies only the adverb it is given. Unseen objects, sensor recalibration and gel wear go untested everywhere.
  • Underpowered evaluation. UniVTAC and N0-Foundation each run 20 real trials per task, and Tabero reports no trial count at all. None reports seeds or confidence intervals. SoftVTBench flags its single training run.
  • No force ground truth on hardware. The two suites that reach real robots score binary success and visual milestones, so the gentleness and deformation compliance their simulated metrics reward go unmeasured.
  • No perturbation tests. None of the four bumps an object or induces a slip mid-rollout, which is what would show whether a policy uses touch to correct rather than to classify.

Where the field stands

Four surveys published this year read the same way. Contact-rich manipulation has plenty of demonstrations and plenty of hardware, and almost nothing transfers between them.

The dexterous-hand survey [1] tabulates 29 hands and finds they “span a wide range of design envelopes rather than converging on a single best architecture”, while the vision-based tactile survey [2] catalogues about 100 sensor variants. Of the 53 force- and tactile-aware learning methods surveyed by Shan et al. [4], 25 carry a force/torque or joint-torque sensor and 27 carry a tactile sensor, but only 4 carry both.

Two principles do the sorting, both read off what contact is physically, a partially observable hybrid system whose mode switches discontinuously.

  • Information During contact the decisive variables, slip, normal and shear force, and contact patch, are observable only through contact, so any pipeline that treats touch as auxiliary to vision inverts the hierarchy at the moment it matters most.
  • Timescale Contact switches in milliseconds while task semantics evolve over seconds, so a split between a slow reasoner and a fast loop is forced by the physics rather than chosen for convenience.

Six directions, ranked by how much they unlock. Each tag names a row of the table: solid removes that problem, outlined only eases it.

  1. Physically grounded contact targets Train encoders whose targets are contact force and torque, contact geometry and slip state, with sensor-specific heads, rather than pretraining on each sensor’s raw images. GenForce already maps heterogeneous signals into a shared marker space, which is the same move one level lower.fixes no shared contact representationeases expensive tactile dataeases misaligned modalitieseases unsolved tactile sim-to-real
  2. A control contract Have the slow policy emit what a fast controller consumes, a reference force and torque, impedance targets and contact-phase intent. Shan et al. name these intermediate modalities but note they are “meaningful only when the robot exposes a matching control mode”, which is the gap a standard interface would close.fixes no reasoner-controller contracteases misaligned modalities
  3. Touch and force as intrinsic critics Predict how contact will evolve, then treat the gap between predicted and observed contact as evidence that execution was physically wrong. The direction is Shan et al.’ own, not ours.eases expensive tactile dataeases no reliability scoring
  4. Compliance as a design variable Passive mechanical compliance lowers the bandwidth and precision the control loop has to deliver. The hand survey co-designs sensing with actuation, but not compliance with the learned policy.fixes hardware trade-offseases no reasoner-controller contract
  5. Physics-calibrated simulation Calibrate contact and deformation against small real datasets, then generate data in the physical representation rather than in sensor-image space. DiffTactile is differentiable and Taccel is GPU-parallel, so both can carry that load.eases expensive tactile datafixes unsolved tactile sim-to-real
  6. Reliability benchmarks and better demonstrations Score force safety, contact stability, recovery and sensor failure, and give demonstrators tactile feedback so that what gets recorded is worth imitating.fixes touchless demonstrationsfixes no reliability scoring

Supporting detail

The four surveys · what each number points to
  • [1] Zhao et al., Towards Robotic Dexterous Hand Intelligence: A Survey Its own prescription cuts against the diversity it documents: modular design with standardised interfaces and plug-and-play components, not task-specific hardware.
  • [2] Zhou et al., Vision-Based Tactile Intelligence for Robotics: Sensing, Learning, and Embodied Manipulation Calls this hardware “task-driven co-design rather than selection of a universal architecture”. It is the survey that cites the tactile backbones Sparsh, T3, AnyTouch and UniT, the policies OmniVTLA, T-Rex and UniTacVLA, and the simulators DiffTactile and Taccel.
  • [3] Cao et al., Tactile-based Multimodal Fusion in Embodied Intelligence: A Survey of Vision, Language, and Contact-Driven Paradigms The clearest statement of the evaluation gap: “no single metric currently captures tactile realism, perceptual plausibility, semantic correctness, and control effectiveness in a unified manner”. Its answer to heterogeneity is unified tactile tokenisation, which is a learned sensor-agnostic token rather than a physical quantity.
  • [4] Shan et al., Learning Physical Interaction: A Survey of Tactile- and Force-aware Robot Learning The only one to count integration directly; the four methods that pair both sensors are RDP, TACT, TaF-VLA and MoDE-VLA. It supplies the latency tension, the intermediate-modality taxonomy and the reliability-benchmark list.
What we would not work on · three directions that fight the wrong variable
  • Another sensor variant. With no shared representation to report into, the next one adds hardware diversity rather than capability.
  • A monolithic policy with touch as one more token. The timescale principle says the ceiling here is structural, so scale does not move it.
  • Appearance-level sim-to-real. Translating one sensor’s pixels matches the variable we do not need, while the physics underneath is the one that transfers.
